# Dynamo and electric motor (`dynamo_electric_motor`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electromagnetism; helped by ohms_law_circuits, wire_drawing, water_wheel, steam_turbine, water_turbine
- Core idea: A coil of insulated wire turned between the poles of a magnet has a current induced in it that reverses every half turn. A commutator, a split copper ring on the shaft touched by two fixed brushes, switches the connections at the right moment so that direct current comes out. The same machine fed with current turns as a motor. Large output needs electromagnets instead of permanent magnets, fed by part of the machine's own current: the weak magnetism left in the iron starts the process (self-excitation). The rotating iron must be built up from thin insulated sheets or wires, or it heats and wastes the power, and the air gap between rotor and poles must be small.
- Pitfalls:
  - Forgetting the commutator and wondering why no steady direct current appears
  - A solid iron rotor: eddy currents heat it and eat most of the power
  - Building an electric motor first and running it from batteries; zinc burnt in cells cost many times as much as coal burnt under a boiler, which is why motors waited for the dynamo
  - Believing a motor driving a dynamo that feeds the motor could run for ever
  - Short-circuiting a running dynamo, or opening the field circuit of a large machine, which gives a dangerous high-voltage arc
- History: europe: 1821 – Faraday's rotation experiment; 1831 Faraday's disc; 1832 Pixii's hand-cranked magneto with commutator; 1834–1838 Jacobi's motor drives a boat in St Petersburg; c. 1861 Jedlik notes self-excitation but does not publish; 1866–1867 self-excited dynamo (Werner Siemens, Wheatstone, Varley, independently); 1871 Gramme's ring dynamo; 1873 Vienna exhibition shows the dynamo running as a motor; americas: 1837 – Davenport's patent for a battery motor; 1880s Edison and Sprague develop efficient dynamos and traction motors
- Read:
  - Michael Faraday, Experimental Researches in Electricity, vol. 1 (1839)
  - Brian Bowers, A History of Electric Light and Power (1982)
